new_statements.quote: 臺灣の土蕃語は、各部族を通じ、其音調は、概して中調平直にして、著しき昂低抑揚の差なく、……而して此音調の昂揚は、二熟音に成れる語詞に在りては、最初の熟音に表出し、多熟音に成れる語詞に在りては、最終熟音の一位を上れる熟音 (Penultima) に表出するを常とす。(附考) 蕃語の特徴は、音調概して平直なるを常とするも、除外の例として、罕に支那の漢語の四聲の別の如く、同一語として、音調の昂上及び低下の差により、全く意義を異にすること無きにあらず、プユマ部族語の、左の三例の如きは、其適例にして
new_statements.translation: In the native languages of Taiwan, through all the tribes, the pitch is on the whole mid and level, without marked differences of high and low modulation, ... and this raising of the pitch, in words consisting of two syllables, appears on the first syllable, and in words consisting of many syllables, appears as a rule on the syllable one position above the final syllable (Penultima). (Note) Although it is the rule that the pitch of the aboriginal languages is level, as an exception, rarely, like the four-tone distinction of Chinese, one and the same word may differ entirely in meaning by the difference of rising and falling pitch; the three examples from the Puyuma tribal language at left are cases in point
new_statements.citation: 伊能嘉矩 (Ino, Kanori). 1916. 臺灣土蕃語の特徴に就き (一) [On the characteristics of the native languages of Taiwan, part 1]. 人類學雜誌 (Journal of the Anthropological Society of Tokyo) 31(6): 215-218. (Parts (二) 31(8): 273ff. and (三) 31(9): 315ff., same year, not downloaded.)
new_statements.locator: 人類學雜誌 31(6), pp. 216 (last column, heading (乙) 音調の特徴) - 217 (lower block, with emphasis circles on 最初の熟音 and 最終熟音の一位を上れる熟音); Malay comparison p. 218 upper block
new_statements.relation_note: Section (乙) 音調の特徴 (pp. 216-218): the pitch/intonation (音調) of the Formosan native languages is, through all tribes, mid and level without marked high-low modulation; a word's pitch is raised (昂揚) for emphasis or linking, and this raising falls on the first syllable of disyllabic words and on the penultimate syllable (Penultima) of polysyllabic words as a rule; note (附考): exceptionally, as in the Chinese four tones, a few word pairs differ in meaning only by rising vs falling pitch, e.g. Puyuma Wade 'tooth' (level) vs Wade 'younger sibling' (falling), Indan 'fearful' (rising) vs Indan 'mouth' (falling), Soan 'horn' (rising) vs Soan 'dog' (falling); p. 218: this penultimate prominence is 'pre…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Pan-Formosan generalization (Ino 1916): prominence (described as a pitch rise) on the penultimate syllable; in disyllables on the first syllable (= penult); otherwise level pitch; no lexical tone except a few pitch-distinguished pairs reported for Puyuma.
new_statements.exceptions: Puyuma word pairs distinguished by rising vs falling pitch (Wade, Indan, Soan); emphasis/linking can raise the pitch of the main word.
new_statements.identity_note: Overview of phonetic characteristics of 'the native languages of Taiwan, through all tribes' by the fieldworker who recorded the Taipei-basin Ketangalan (keta1243) wordlists in 1896-98; p. 216 says he also checked 'the many tribal languages already extinct' (his plains-language records) against Psalmanazar's forgery, so the extinct Pepo are inside his purview, but the accent statement is a pan-Formosan generalization illustrated only with Atayal (Patos-An), Puyuma (pitch pairs), Siraya (fig. 1) and Malay; no Ketangalan/Luilang/Pepo form is cited for accent. Not a languoid-specific statement.

sources.citation: Li, Paul Jen-kuei. 1993. New data on three extinct Formosan languages. BIHP 63.2: 301-323 (reprint in Li 2004, Selected Papers on Formosan Languages vol. 1, 91-108).
sources.note: p. 93 (sec. 2.1 Basay): 'Stress falls on the final syllable.' -- but this is for BASAY (basa1287; the language Abe/Ogawa used to call 'Ketangalan'), from a rememberer recorded in Jilung 1987; it does not cover Taipei-basin Ketangalan/Luilang (keta1243), which Li lists separately as extinct with <100 recorded items.

sources.citation: Li, Paul Jen-kuei & Elizabeth Zeitoun. 2024. Classification of Formosan languages. In Paul Jen-kuei Li, Elizabeth Zeitoun & Rik De Busser (eds.), Handbook of Formosan Languages: The Indigenous Languages of Taiwan, 66-101. Leiden: Brill. (author copy on the ILAS, Academia Sinica researcher page of E. Zeitoun; 37 pp.)
sources.note: No prosodic content for any northern plains language. Phonological material is diachronic and subgroup-diagnostic only (e.g. Western Plains mergers *ŋ/*n > n and *s/*t > t; PAN *C > s and *q > glottal stop in Saisiyat and Kulon-Pazeh; Tsouic loss of final *n 'after an unstressed /a/'; Ross's Puyuma/Rukai vowel reductions 'before stressed syllables'). The words stress/unstressed occur only in those Tsouic/Nuclear-Austronesian arguments (the text), never in connection with Basay, Ketangalan or Luilang.

sources.citation: 李壬癸 (Li, Paul Jen-kuei). 2010. 從文獻資料看台灣平埔族群的語言 [The languages of the Formosan plains peoples as seen from documentary sources]. 臺灣語文研究 (Journal of Taiwanese Languages and Literature) 5(1): 1-14.
sources.note: Phonological content is diachronic only: mergers *n/*ŋ, *s/*t, loss of *k and final *-y (western group); *j/*n merger (Basay, Kavalan, Amis, Siraya); *j,*n,*N merger and *k > k/q split (Basay+Kavalan); Siraya/Taivuan/Makatau correspondences. No synchronic phonology, no 重音/stress or tone remark for any language.

sources.citation: Sagart, Laurent. 2004. The higher phylogeny of Austronesian and the position of Tai-Kadai. Oceanic Linguistics 43(2): 411-444. Author manuscript (HAL halshs-00090906); open mirror copy at Eötvös Loránd University.
sources.note: Only stress content concerns Sagart's PAn reconstruction of *pitu/*walu/*Siwa: 'I arbitrarily assign stress to the penultimate syllable of '7' and to the final syllable in each of '8' and '9'' with fn. 9 'I assume PAn generally had final stress'. No statement about Luilang or Basay prosody.

sources.citation: Li, Paul Jen-kuei (李壬癸). 2001. 巴賽語的地位 [The linguistic position of Basay]. Language and Linguistics 2.2: 155-171.
sources.note: Subgrouping paper; explains that Ino's 'Ketagalan' should properly be called Basay (Mabuchi 1953-4, Tsuchida 1985) and that only a few lexical items survive for the Taipei-basin varieties. Nothing on stress (no 重音).

sources.citation: Wurm, S. A., P. Mühlhäusler & D. T. Tryon (eds.). 1996. Atlas of Languages of Intercultural Communication in the Pacific, Asia, and the Americas (Trends in Linguistics. Documentation 13). Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter. DOI 10.1515/9783110819724. [held page-text, 1903 PDF pages]
sources.note: No phonology at all. Historical-sociolinguistic account: Basay was a lingua franca of the Taipei area in the Spanish period (1626-1642), quoted from Esquivel and de los Angeles via Borao 1993; plains tribes incl. Ketagalan now speak Taiwanese.

sources.citation: Tsuchida, Shigeru. 1985. Kulon: Yet another Austronesian language in Taiwan? Bulletin of the Institute of Ethnology, Academia Sinica 60: 1-59.
sources.note: Comparative wordlist study (Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description, 'wordlist or less'); Ketangalan = wordlists ##17-22 in the appendix. No stress rule anywhere; the only prosodic remark is p. 3 fn. 1: the kana/Chinese-character/roman records left by non-linguists are 'uncertain in regard to the distinction between b/m, l/r, medial and final t/l/r, and stress/length' -- i.e. stress is not recoverable from the surviving Ketangalan data.

sources.citation: 浅井恵倫 (Asai, Erin). 1954. 台湾言語学はどこまで進んだか? [Contributions of Japanese linguists to the study of the Indonesian languages of Formosa]. 民族學研究 (Japanese Journal of Ethnology) 18(1-2): 12-19. (<特集>台湾研究)
sources.note: No phonology of any plains language. States that apart from the 平埔族 language records the old 舊慣調査會 questionnaire returns were discarded, that 'the old informants are now almost all dead', and (general method remark) that without sound analysis words and texts cannot be written in phonetic/phonemic transcription. English summary praises Ogawa's IPA-based dictionaries and his phonological theories (q-sound, *t/*L/*n/*s dualization) -- nothing on accent/stress for Ketangalan.

sources.citation: 馬淵東一 (Mabuchi, Toichi). 1954. 高砂族の分類 : 学史的回顧 [Classification of the Formosan aborigines: a retrospect] (<特集>台湾研究). 民族學研究 (Japanese Journal of Ethnology) 18(1-2): 1-11.
sources.note: no phonology content -- ethnological classification history only (names, locations, authors); no language data beyond ethnonyms.

sources.citation: 臺北帝國大學言語學研究室 編 [小川尚義・淺井惠倫]. 1935. 原語による臺灣高砂族傳說集 [Myths and traditions of the Formosan native tribes (texts in the original languages)]. 東京: 刀江書院. NDL Digital Collections pid 1453611 (public domain, scanned full text).
sources.note: For Ketagalan: nothing -- it is listed under 'III. languages no longer in use, or surviving only in the memory of a few old people'. The two アクセント hits in the volume (frames 28 and 291) belong to the Atayal section and to a phonetic note on an Ami village (パーラン社), not to Ketagalan. Comparative table frame 14 gives Ketagalan numerals (e.g. spat '4') without prosodic marks = wordlist-only data.

sources.citation: Mueller, W. 1910. Ueber die Wildenstaemme der Insel Formosa. Zeitschrift fuer Ethnologie 42: 228-241.
sources.note: Ethnographic overview; language content is one paragraph plus an appendix table of numerals 1-10 for all Formosan groups including a row 'Y) Ketanganan' (Tsa, Rusa..). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Ino, Kanori (伊能嘉矩). 1896-1898. Reports on the Pepo of the Taipei area in 東京人類學會雜誌 [Journal of the Anthropological Society of Tokyo] (e.g. nos. 119-136), with Ketangalan wordlists in kana.
sources.note: The raw wordlists (##17-22 in Tsuchida's appendix) for Taipei-basin Ketangalan; open on J-STAGE but kana transcription cannot encode stress -- listed only for completeness of the primary record.

sources.citation: 伊能嘉矩 (Ino, Kanori). n.d. [c. 1896-1900]. 舊淡水縣十九社平埔蕃語一覽表 [Vocabulary table of the plains-aborigine language of the nineteen villages of old Tamsui county] and 同 增補 [supplement]. Manuscript charts (71x71 cm; 80x125 cm), 伊能文庫 M049-1/M049-2 (series 蕃語彙集(一): ペイポ族ノ部, accession 1607443), National Taiwan University Library; Ino Kanori Manuscripts digital archive items 874662 and 874664 (IIIF).
sources.note: Nothing: bare comparative vocabulary chart (numerals, 百/千/萬, body parts, kin, nature, animals, '其の記憶に存する各種の語') in roman letters with sporadic unexplained macron/breve/circumflex marks (tôoru, Pitôo, siwăt, supăt); no legend or prose on either sheet.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid record keta1243 + English Wikipedia 'Luilang language', 'Basay language', 'Ketagalan people'.
sources.note: Identity only: Glottolog links keta1243 to Wikipedia 'Luilang language', Glottolog's most extensive descriptions = Tsuchida 1985 and Mueller 1910 (both 'wordlist or less'), 0 descriptive refs. Wikipedia: 'probably went extinct in the mid-20th century and it is little researched'; only numerals (Guerin, Ino, Ogawa) cited. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Li, Paul Jen-kuei. 2024. Basay. In Li, Zeitoun & De Busser (eds.), Handbook of Formosan Languages: The Indigenous Languages of Taiwan. Leiden: Brill.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Most recent synthesis of all northern plains (Basay/Trobiawan/Ketangalan-Luilang) materials; if any modern author comments on prosody of the Taipei-basin variety or explicitly extends the Basay final-stress statement to it, it would be here. Low odds: Luilang data are <100 kana-recorded items.
